subject: Medical Triads
title: Beck, Cushing and Virchow Triads: What They Mean—and What They Do Not
preview: A compact high-yield guide to classic cardiovascular and neurological triads, with clinical interpretation and common exam traps.
body:
• Beck's Triad (Cardiac Tamponade): 1. Hypotension, 2. Muffled heart sounds, 3. Distended Jugular Vein (JVD). Pathophysiology: Fluid in pericardial sac restricts heart filling, dropping stroke volume.
  • Cushing's Triad (Raised Intracranial Pressure): 1. Hypertension (with widened pulse pressure), 2. Bradycardia, 3. Irregular respiration (Cheyne-Stokes). Clue: It's a late, ominous sign of brain herniation.
  • Virchow's Triad (DVT / Pulmonary Embolism): 1. Venous stasis (bedridden), 2. Endothelial injury (surgery/trauma), 3. Hypercoagulability (Factor V Leiden, OCPs, Cancer).
  • Wernicke's Triad (Thiamine Deficiency): 1. Confusion (Encephalopathy), 2. Oculomotor dysfunction (Nystagmus/CN VI palsy), 3. Ataxia. Treatment: ALWAYS give IV Thiamine BEFORE Glucose.

sections.title: Beck's triad: cardiac tamponade
points: Classical features: hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds.
The full triad may be absent, particularly in slowly developing tamponade; absence does not exclude the condition.
Interpret findings with hemodynamics and appropriate echocardiography when clinically indicated.

sections.title: Cushing's triad: raised intracranial pressure
points: Traditional teaching combines hypertension with widened pulse pressure, bradycardia and abnormal respirations.
It is a late warning pattern associated with serious intracranial hypertension; do not wait for all components before recognizing deterioration.

sections.title: Virchow's triad: thrombosis
points: The three thrombosis-promoting factors are endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow (stasis) and hypercoagulability.
Virchow’s triad describes mechanisms and risk factors, not a bedside diagnostic test for an acute pulmonary embolism.

sections.title: Differentiate by clinical problem
points: Beck → obstructive cardiac filling / tamponade clues.
Cushing → possible dangerously raised intracranial pressure.

sections.title: INI-CET-style pitfalls
points: A classic triad is a memory aid, not a requirement for diagnosis.
Prioritize clinical urgency and context over remembering isolated names.

quiz.question: Which combination is the classic Beck triad?
options: Hypotension, elevated JVP and muffled heart sounds
Fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain
quiz.explanation: Beck’s triad describes tamponade; it is not consistently present.

quiz.question: Which is NOT part of Virchow’s triad?
quiz.explanation: Virchow’s triad includes injury, stasis and hypercoagulability.

quiz.question: If the classic Beck triad is absent, what is the most appropriate interpretation?
quiz.explanation: The full triad has limited sensitivity and should not be used alone to rule out tamponade.

rapidRevision: Beck: low BP + high JVP + quiet heart sounds (not always all present).
Cushing: hypertension + bradycardia + abnormal breathing is a late sign.
